--- title: "Kinds of marine data" description: "Continuous, categorical, circular, temporal, spatial, profile and compositional data, and what each one needs before a model can use it." order: 2 categories: [data-preparation, marine-data] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## A model sees only numbers A model does not know that one column is a month and another a position on a map. It sees numbers and does arithmetic on them, whatever they mean. Knowing what kind of variable each column holds lets you hand it to a model in a form where that arithmetic makes sense, and spot a column that would mislead it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Marine data holds seven kinds of variable Most introductions stop at two kinds, numbers and categories. Marine data has more: ::: {.diagram} ![Seven kinds of variable common in marine data, with examples of each and what it needs before a model can use it.](img/data-kinds.svg){fig-alt="Seven cards. Continuous: temperature, depth, salinity; needs scaling. Categorical: substrate, gear type, vessel; needs encoding as numbers. Circular: month, season, bearing, tidal phase; needs sine and cosine. Temporal: sampling dates and times; needs a known date format. Spatial: longitude, latitude; needs splits by area. Profile: a CTD cast, values down the water; needs one summary per cast. Compositional: species shares, grain-size fractions; needs log-ratios."} ::: A **continuous variable** is a measured quantity, where a difference of one unit means the same everywhere on the scale: temperature, depth, salinity. A **categorical variable** puts each row into one of a fixed set of groups: a seabed type, a vessel. [Scaling and encoding](scaling-and-encoding.qmd) puts continuous columns on a common scale, which methods that measure distance need, and turns categories into numbers. The rest of this page covers the kinds that are easy to get wrong. ## A number is not always a quantity A column stored as numbers is not necessarily a quantity. Seabed types are often recorded as codes: 1 for sand, 2 for mud, 3 for gravel, 4 for rock. A model given that column treats rock as four times sand and gravel as halfway between mud and rock, and fits a trend through codes someone chose. Categories come in two kinds. A **nominal** category has no order: sand, mud, gravel, rock. An **ordinal** category has an order but no known spacing: a disturbance score of low, medium or high. Coding it 1, 2, 3 claims that medium sits exactly halfway between the other two, which is a guess. ## Cycles belong on a circle A **circular variable** returns to where it started: month, day of the year, tidal phase, current direction, time of day. December is month 12 and January month 1: eleven apart on a number line, but neighbours in the ocean. The usual fix replaces the column with two new ones, its sine and cosine, which place each value on a circle: $$x_1 = \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right), \qquad x_2 = \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right)$$ where $t$ is the position in the cycle and $T$ its length: 12 for months, 365 for days of the year, 360 for a bearing in degrees. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} months <- tibble( month = 1:12, name = month.abb, x = sin(2 * pi * month / 12), y = cos(2 * pi * month / 12) ) p_line <- ggplot(months, aes(month, 0)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#d7dde2") + geom_point(size = 3, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + geom_text(aes(label = name), vjust = -1.4, size = 3.2) + annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 12, y = -0.35, yend = -0.35, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 0.8, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) + annotate("text", x = 6.5, y = -0.5, label = "The model thinks these are 11 apart", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.4) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.7, 0.5)) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 12, 2)) + labs(x = "Month number", y = NULL, title = "As a raw number") + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) p_circle <- ggplot(months, aes(x, y)) + geom_path(data = tibble(x = sin(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)), y = cos(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200))), colour = "#d7dde2") + geom_point(size = 3, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + geom_text(aes(label = name, x = x * 1.18, y = y * 1.18), size = 3.2) + annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "Dec and Jan\nare neighbours", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.4) + coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.35, 1.35), ylim = c(-1.35, 1.35)) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "As sine and cosine") + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) p_line + p_circle ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The same twelve months, encoded two ways. On a number line December and January sit at opposite ends; on a circle they are neighbours, as they are in the ocean.](marine-data-types_files/figure-html/fig-circular-1.png){#fig-circular fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel places months 1 to 12 along a straight horizontal line, with a long arrow showing the distance of 11 between December and January. The right panel places the same months around a circle, with December and January adjacent.' width=1700} ::: ::: The encoding spends two columns on one variable and assumes the cycle is smooth. A quantity that jumps at a boundary, such as a quota year that starts in April, does not belong on a circle. ## Dates need a known format Dates arrive as text, in whatever format the logging software wrote. The survey's two vessels used two formats: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw <- load_coastal_survey_raw() raw |> distinct(vessel, sample_date) |> slice_head(n = 2, by = vessel) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|vessel |sample_date | |:----------|:-----------| |RV Kaiyo |2022-04-21 | |RV Kaiyo |2022-10-21 | |RV Tsubasa |05/10/2022 | |RV Tsubasa |15/01/2019 |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_raw raw = load_coastal_survey_raw() raw[["vessel", "sample_date"]].drop_duplicates().groupby("vessel").head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | vessel | sample_date | |---:|:-----------|:--------------| | 0 | RV Kaiyo | 2022-04-21 | | 1 | RV Kaiyo | 2022-10-21 | | 3 | RV Tsubasa | 05/10/2022 | | 6 | RV Tsubasa | 15/01/2019 | ::: ::: ::: A date such as `05/10/2022` is 5 October in most of the world and 10 May in the United States, and nothing in the text says which. Read the wrong way, it moves a station into another season without any error. So find out which format each source used, and parse each format explicitly: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dated <- raw |> mutate( sample_date = coalesce(ymd(sample_date, quiet = TRUE), dmy(sample_date, quiet = TRUE)), day_of_year = yday(sample_date) ) sum(is.na(dated$sample_date)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # One vessel logged ISO dates, the other day-first. Parse each format on its # own and take whichever succeeded, rather than letting pandas guess per row. iso = pd.to_datetime(raw["sample_date"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce") dayfirst = pd.to_datetime(raw["sample_date"], format="%d/%m/%Y", errors="coerce") dated = raw.assign(sample_date=iso.fillna(dayfirst)) dated["day_of_year"] = dated["sample_date"].dt.dayofyear int(dated["sample_date"].isna().sum()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: No date is left unparsed, and `day_of_year` is ready for the sine and cosine above. ## Time and position say which rows are alike Time and position can be inputs, but they matter more for another reason: they say which rows are close to each other, and so likely to be alike. Samples a day apart, or a few kilometres apart, share information, as repeat visits to one site do ([The coastal survey](the-coastal-survey.qmd#the-stations-come-from-far-fewer-sites)). That limits how the data can be split to test a model, which [Splitting the data](splitting-data.qmd) takes up. As inputs, longitude and latitude often improve predictions while explaining nothing, because they stand in for whatever the other columns missed, just as salinity stood in for depth in [Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd). Variables built from position, such as distance to the coast or the slope of the seabed, are usually more useful than raw coordinates. ## Profiles and shares need reshaping A **profile** is a series of measurements down the water at one place and time, such as a CTD cast: a curve, not a single row. The usual start is one row per cast, with summaries chosen for the biology: surface temperature, mixed layer depth, total chlorophyll. Splitting a cast into one row per depth band instead multiplies rows that are not independent, so a cast's rows must then stay together when the data are split. **Compositional data** are shares of a whole, such as the proportion of each species in a sample, and sum to one: if one share rises, others must fall. Methods that ignore this can report links between shares that come from the arithmetic, not the ecology. The usual remedy is a **log-ratio**, the log of each share divided by another share or by their average, which removes the sum-to-one constraint. ## The kinds in the survey The raw survey file holds five of the seven kinds in its 17 columns, plus identifiers and outcomes: | Kind or role | Columns | Stored as | Before a model uses it | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Continuous | `depth_m`, `temperature_c`, `salinity_psu`, `chlorophyll_mg_m3` | numbers | A common scale, for methods that measure distance | | Categorical | `vessel`, `substrate` | text | Dummy columns ([Scaling and encoding](scaling-and-encoding.qmd)) | | Circular | `season` | text | Sine and cosine of `day_of_year`, or four categories | | Temporal | `sample_date`, `survey_year` | text; whole numbers | Parse each date format explicitly | | Spatial | `longitude`, `latitude` | numbers | Mostly for splitting by place | | Identifiers | `station_id`, `site_id` | text | Never an input; `site_id` keeps a site's rows together | | Outcomes | `abundance`, `present`, `rare_species`, `catch_weight_kg` | numbers; text | What a model predicts, never an input | Two columns are easy to misread. `season` stored as text looks like four unrelated categories and hides that spring comes between winter and summer. `catch_weight_kg` is a number like any other, but it is weighed from the same catch that is counted, so it is another measure of the outcome; [Avoiding information leakage](information-leakage.qmd) shows what happens when a model is given it. Nothing in the file says either: knowing what a column means is knowledge you bring. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A model does arithmetic on whatever it is given; a column stored as numbers is not necessarily a quantity. - Circular variables such as month, bearing and tidal phase need sine and cosine, or December ends up far from January. - Ambiguous date formats silently move stations between seasons: find out the format and parse it explicitly. - Time and position say which rows are alike, which limits how the data can be split. - Profiles need summarising, usually one row per cast; compositional shares need log-ratios. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Encode `day_of_year` as sine and cosine, and plot `abundance` against each. Does the seasonal pattern look clearer than against `season` as four categories? 2. List the columns in your own data and write next to each what it *means*, not how it is stored. How many are circular, compositional, or a name stored as a number?
